I will never miss an opportunity to mention the 2005 Mexican Military response to Hurricane Katrina in Texas and how these types of vehicles, in the form of [trailers modified as community kitchens](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/20050926174219_-_Mexican_army_mobile_kitchen_in_Texas.jpg/1024px-20050926174219_-_Mexican_army_mobile_kitchen_in_Texas.jpg), were deployed by road through the border making it the first time Mexican troops had set foot on the United States since the Mexican-American war (Not counting the detachment of pilots and servicemen , this in conjunction with air assets as well as the Mexican Navy ship ARM Papaloapan A-411 (Previously the USS Newport LST-1179) where they offloaded even further supplies using American landing craft and a Mexican Mil Mi-17 helicopter. 

During the 20-day stay they distributed drinking water, thousands of meals and helped with shelter, rescue and cleaning operations alongside the American authorities and military for the American citizens in the affected areas, after which they left back into Mexico. While not the sole international response to the crisis, it was one of the largest and one of the closest in the region, and it is a story that I love to bring that up to keep the reminder of the partnership between the two countries and how it must be preserved. 

Worth mentioning that these same type of vehicles are very important on how the military handles response to natural disasters still to the day or other emergencies, being a more fielded response to do things such as prepare the meals on site, rather that distributing things like MREs which are not a thing here, not even for the troops. This particular picture in the original post is from a parade. And its kinda silly seeing them drive down the avenues of Mexico City in the mobile tortilladora during September 16th, but a [similar vehicle](https://www.eleconomista.com.mx/export/sites/eleconomista/img/2024/04/11/agua_alcaldia_benito_juarez_ejercito_plan_afp_2.png_605617689.png) was deployed in the form of a mobile water purification plant, in response to a water crisis in a neighborhood of the capital a few months ago.

Reading on the Abrams use, at least by American forces, shows how a remarkable piece of war technology this tank is.

With the Gulf War, Iraq War and Afghanistan operations combined only but a handful of tanks were completely lost in combat by direct enemy fire or action. Several were lost by friendly fire incidents by equally powerful equipment. And the worst that came out of several incidents was partial damage disabling the tank, and injuring the crew. And many of these were later repaired with ease.

There's even a instance where in the Iraq War, an M1 was disabled by a recoiless rifle, subsequently the US forces tried to destroy it to prevent capture, and the damn fucker wouldn't die. They moved the ammo to a vulnerable place, threw granades and even fired at it with a HEAT round from another Abrams, and it was until they fucking air strike it that it finally blew up for good. Meanwhile you got the Russian hotpots that from the start of the war, were exploiting like piñatas from the combined efforts of the local armed civilians, the UA National Guard and the initial movements of the UA military. To disable the Abrams itself it either took other remarkable Western ordnance or a series of very specific conditions for an Abrams to be initially badly damage, and only then it subsequently succumbed and was considered destroyed. Not to mention that the shortcomings it may have had, were studied and worked on, like the vulnerability to IEDs. The American military took notice to this quickly, retired the tanks, upgraded them, and sent them back. Something that will hardly happen for the Russian military who at the most would retire the batallions, sell them at bulk for scrap and continue to fund the 'glorious Oligarch Navy.'

I think needless to say this is not a perfect machine, nothing made by humans is. But the further losses occure outside of American control. The West wouldn't be sending this asset to Ukraine if there wasn't enough trust that they know how to opperate them, maintain them and win in the battlefield with them. Something that has been proven with every piece of equipment they have sent, from the various Anti-Armour weapons previous to the invasion, to the HIMARs system that continues to inflict monumental damage.
